extracted.intended_audience: educators, educational theorists, teachers, and students of education
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical principles for schooling that treat education as growth: criteria for habit-formation, the role of plasticity and dependence, and critiques of alternative conceptions (preparation, unfolding, formal discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plasticity (capacity to learn from experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plasticity is the specific adaptability of an immature creature for growth — the ability to learn from experience; the power to retain from one experience something which is of avail in coping with the difficulties of a later situation; power to modify actions on the basis of the results of prior experiences; the power to develop dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not the same as putty-like malleability; lies near pliable elasticity but is deeper. Enables the acquisition of habits and 'the habit of learning' (learning to learn). Examples: human infants require extended practice to coordinate sight and reaching, so plasticity enables flexible control across situations rather than being limited by fixed endowment (as in a chick). Emphasize experiences that allow carry-over and transfer; protect and prolong plasticity (e.g., through longer dependency phases) to support continued growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence / need for others as educational resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of dependent and learning beings (prolonged infancy) is a stimulus to nurture and affection and plays a crucial role in forming habits of sympathetic watchfulness, foresight, planning, and other social virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prolongation of dependence prolongs plasticity and opportunity for social and intellectual development. Adult responsibilities should not be imposed prematurely; the social context of care fosters dispositions essential to associated life and further social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits as expressions of growth — executive skill and control of environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A habit is a form of executive skill, an ability to use natural conditions as means to ends; an active control of the environment through control of the organs of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of habits lies in the economical and effective control of the environment they secure (e.g., walking, talking, playing an instrument, professional skills). Education should form habits that enable purposeful transformation and use of surroundings — not merely internal changes in the organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between habituation (passive conformity) and active habits (adaptive control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habituation is a relatively passive enduring adjustment (getting used to surroundings) supplying a background equilibrium, whereas active habits are capacities to readjust activity to meet new conditions and to transform the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating all habits with passive accommodation. Ensure instruction cultivates selective responsiveness and the ability to modify actions, not mere acceptance of fixed environmental conditions. Use background habituation as leverage for targeted active adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits include intellectual and emotional dispositions, not just motor skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits involve intellectual elements (acquaintance with materials, ways of understanding situations) and emotional inclinations (active preference and choice) as well as motor competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop habits of mind (judging, reasoning, observation, reflection) alongside manual or motor skills. Higher-grade habits integrate intellectual factors and supply significance and flexible use; curricular design should foster both technical skill and accompanying cognitive/emotional dispositions (e.g., engineers' or physicians' modes of thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity of habit versus flexibility — danger of routine and enslavement
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixity of habit can mean resources always available, but also ruts and routine ways with loss of freshness, open-mindedness, and originality; 'bad' habits are those severed from reason and opposed to deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against habits that close off plasticity. Design experiences that keep intelligence engaged so habits remain resources rather than chains. Identify and counter routine, unthinking practices that produce arrested development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoke intelligence in habit formation; avoid mere mechanical drill
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of valuable habits requires the function of intelligence to be invoked to its maximum; reliance on mechanical routine and repetition to secure external efficiency without thought closes in surroundings upon growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: short-sighted drill that produces motor skill without accompanying thought; using repetition as a substitute for reflective, thoughtful practice. Instead, combine practice with intellectual engagement, invention, and initiative so habits support continued growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as development — continuous growth and self-end
rubrics_metrics.description: If education is development, the educational process has no end beyond itself; it is its own end and is one of continual reorganizing, reconstructing, and transforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational success should be judged by how much schooling creates a desire for continued growth and supplies means to make that desire effective. Organize schooling to foster lifelong inclination to learn rather than to finish a preparatory task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'education as preparation' — avoid making future the primary motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing education primarily as preparation for adult life or some distant future produces loss of impetus, procrastination, reliance on average conventional standards instead of individual strengths/needs, and dependence on extrinsic rewards and punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize present experience — make the present situation educative and motivating. Use present, meaningful ends rather than vague future promises to drive learning. Tailor expectations to individual capacities rather than generic future-oriented averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'education as unfolding toward a fixed goal' (unfolding/transcendental ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceiving development as the unfolding of latent powers toward a fixed, perfect goal substitutes an abstract, external standard for present growth and often results in adult-imposed symbolism, dictation of technique, and suppression of individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the adult ideal or abstract absolutes as the immediate criterion for pedagogical decisions. Beware pedagogical devices that 'draw out' predetermined content (e.g., symbolic schemes) rather than fostering experimental, situational growth. Examples: limitations in Froebel's symbolism and Hegelian institutional-step models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for immaturity — treat manifestations as signs of growth, not ends or nuisances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat native instincts merely as nuisances to suppress nor indulge them as ends in themselves; manifestations of youth are signs of nascent powers to be turned into means of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers and parents should identify impulses that are moving toward development and channel them into constructive activities; excessive attention to surface phenomena (either rebuke or encouragement) risks fixation and arrested development. Balance respect for a child's nature with disciplined guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of school education: create desire and means for continued growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The criterion of the value of school education is the extent in which it creates a desire for continued growth and supplies means for making the desire effective in fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess curricula and pedagogy by their ability to foster intrinsic motivation for lifelong learning and by the concrete opportunities they provide for continued development beyond school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal discipline / training of faculties (perceiving, retaining, thinking, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of formal discipline holds that education should directly train certain faculties (perceiving, retaining, recalling, associating, attending, willing, feeling, imagining, thinking) by graded, repeated exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a historically influential conception (Lockean form); the text critiques it as a 'short cut' that assumes those powers preexist in crude form and can be perfected merely by repetition. Use with caution: ensure that exercise of faculties is embedded in meaningful, growth-oriented activity rather than abstract drill divorced from purpose.
